title: Calorie Deficit Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Calorie Deficit Calculator: Your daily calorie target for a chosen deficit — with a safety check. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example…
content:
The [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Your daily calorie target for a chosen deficit — with a safety check. Enter your sex, age, height, weight, activity level and daily calorie deficit and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Work out how many calories to eat each day to lose weight at the rate you choose. The calculator finds your maintenance calories from the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, then subtracts your chosen daily deficit — one kilogram of body fat stores about 7,700 kcal, so a 500 kcal daily deficit loses about 0.5 kg a week. A target under 1,200 kcal a day (women) or 1,500 kcal (men) is flagged: that low should only be planned with a professional. This is an estimate for healthy adults, not medical advice. It does not suit children, pregnancy, eating disorders or anyone with a medical condition — talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before changing your diet or sleep habits.

## How to use the Calorie Deficit Calculator

Start by choosing your sex from the list, then entering your age, entering your height (cm), entering your weight (kg), choosing your activity level from the list and finally choosing your daily calorie deficit from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your sex, age, height, weight and activity level.
2. Choose your daily deficit — 500 kcal is the usual steady rate.
3. Read your daily calorie target and check the safety note.

## Formula

BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor): men 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5; women the same with −161. Maintenance = BMR × activity factor. Target = maintenance − deficit. Weekly loss = deficit × 7 ÷ 7,700 kg.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 30-year-old man, 180 cm, 90 kg, moderately active, with a 500 kcal deficit: maintenance is 2,914 kcal a day, the target is 2,414 kcal a day, and the expected loss is about 0.45 kg a week. Try the same figures in the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Sex: Male, Age: 30, Height: 180 cm, Weight: 90 kg, Activity level: Moderate (3–5 days/week), Daily calorie deficit: 500 kcal (steady — about 0.5 kg/week)), the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) returns Daily calorie target: 2,414 kcal, Maintenance calories: 2,914 kcal / day, Daily deficit: 500 kcal, Expected loss: About 0.45 kg / week, Safety check: Within the usual safe range. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Why 500 kcal is the usual deficit

A 500 kcal daily deficit adds up to 3,500 kcal a week, which is roughly 0.45 kg of fat — fast enough to see progress, small enough to sustain. Bigger deficits work faster on paper but are harder to live with: hunger, tiredness and muscle loss all rise, and most people give up. A deficit you can keep for months beats a bigger one you keep for a week.

## Why the scale does not fall in a straight line

Water, glycogen and food in the gut can swing your weight by a kilogram day to day, and as you get lighter your maintenance calories fall, so the same target produces a smaller deficit over time. Weigh yourself at the same time of day several times a week and trust the trend over two or three weeks, not any single reading — and re-run this calculator every few kilograms.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- 500 kcal a day is the usual steady deficit — about 0.5 kg a week.
- Weigh yourself several times a week and trust the trend, not one reading.
- Re-run the numbers every few kilograms — maintenance falls as you lose.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a calorie deficit?

Eating fewer calories than your body burns in a day. The shortfall is covered by stored fat, so you lose weight. A 500 kcal daily deficit loses about 0.5 kg a week. Try it with your own numbers in the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How big should my calorie deficit be?

500 kcal a day is the usual steady choice. 250 is gentler, 750–1,000 is the maximum most people should attempt — and only if the target stays above 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 kcal (men). Try it with your own numbers in the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why is my target below 1,200 calories flagged?

Below 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 kcal (men) a day it is hard to get enough nutrients, and the plan should be supervised by a doctor or dietitian. Try it with your own numbers in the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How fast will I lose weight?

Roughly deficit × 7 ÷ 7,700 kg a week — 500 kcal a day is about 0.45 kg a week. Water weight makes the first weeks look faster, then it settles. Try it with your own numbers in the [Calorie Deficit Calculator](/calorie-deficit-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
